sections.title: Name and identification
sections.text: This entry uses the name Russula olivacea Pers. (1796), in the family Russulaceae. European literature also sometimes cites “R. olivacea (Schaeff.) Fr.”; Species Fungorum marks that combination illegitimate and points to Russula roseola, while Persoon’s name is recorded separately. As with other brittlegills, a photograph and cap colour alone are not enough for a secure identification; spore print, chemical reagents and microscopy may be needed.

sections.title: Cap and form
sections.text: This is a large, robust and fleshy brittlegill, with a cap that may reach about 20 cm across. It starts convex, then expands and may become depressed at the centre. The cuticle is matte, often finely concentrically wrinkled or cracked. Colours are highly variable: purple, vinaceous red or reddish-brown mixed with olive, sometimes almost entirely green. The stem is thick and white, often flushed pink to lilac at least in its upper part; it may yellow with age.

sections.title: Gills, flesh and spores
sections.text: The gills are pale to cream at first, then ochre-yellow and sometimes orange-reflecting; their edges may be tinged red near the cap margin. The flesh is firm and white, with a mild taste and faint odour, sometimes described as slightly fruity. The spore print is ochre-yellow. Spores are about 9–11 × 8–9 µm in the Société Mycologique du Nord de la France description, with isolated spines.

sections.title: Habitat and food-safety context
sections.text: Russula olivacea is ectomycorrhizal, most often reported with beech and sometimes with spruce. French accounts report fruiting from summer into autumn; altitude and frequency vary regionally. It has caused gastrointestinal poisonings. The two 2015 ANSES opinions are not worded identically: the risk assessment describes cases mainly after raw or insufficiently cooked meals, while the opinion on a proposed list of edible mushrooms notes reports even after cooking and says no particular treatment has been shown to eliminate the risk. In France, the 5 August 2016 order provided, for one year, for suspending consumer sales of fresh mushrooms without clear information requiring thorough cooking; this temporary measure by itself does not establish a current general ban. The Swiss VAPKO 2023 list still notes possible symptoms and recommends at least 20 minutes of cooking: that is Swiss guidance, not French law or a guarantee of safety.

traits: Large, fleshy brittlegill with a matte cap that may approach 20 cm and develop concentric wrinkles or cracks
Highly variable cap colours: vinaceous red, purple or reddish-brown mixed with olive, sometimes almost wholly green
Cream gills becoming ochre-yellow, sometimes orange-reflecting, with edges that may redden near the margin
Thick white stem, often flushed pink to lilac beneath the gills or in its upper part; firm pale flesh
Ochre-yellow spore print; spores ornamented with isolated spines
Ectomycorrhizal, most often reported under beech and sometimes spruce; observed in summer and autumn
safetyNote: Gastrointestinal poisonings have been reported with Russula olivacea. The 2015 ANSES opinions differ in how they describe cooking, and one says no particular treatment has been shown to eliminate the risk. The French order of 5 August 2016 provided a temporary one-year marketing measure, not a general current ban. VAPKO in Switzerland recommends at least 20 minutes of cooking; this is not French law or a safety guarantee. Do not eat it based on a photo or this entry.
